stories.title: The Rope-Singer's Gambit
stories.text: Before the Remaking, she had sung merchant-songs—trade-tongue rhyming couplets that moved cargo across the Pelimor River and sealed contracts without ledgers. Now, with gold dust blowing through every market, the old songs were the only currency that still held weight. The Dominion auditors had closed the Cordwainer Quarter's docks three weeks prior, claiming consciousness-fragments had been smuggled through the rope-works. Twelve dockmen arrested. Families scattered. The rope-masters who once employed singers like Minda now worked under auditor supervision, their craft reduced to lock-songs and ledger-binding. Minda had come to remake the covenant. She found work at the Frayed Knot, a tavern sunk into the quarter's oldest warehouse, where rope-traders still gathered in whispered circles. They watched her weave braided cords while she hummed—fragments of the old merchant-songs, pitched low enough that only the rope-remembers. On the third night, old Kerwin, a master-knotter whose hands shook with arthritis, approached with a proposition. "The auditors have forbidden us to sing. But ropes have memory, girl. They remember every knot, every cargo, every voice that touched them.

stories.title: The Wyvern's Census
stories.text:
Kolrith the Wise had ruled the Eastern peaks for nine centuries before the Luminous Ascension transformed his three-hundred-year hoard into glittering ash. Now, at the threshold of his final age, the ancient wyvern descended from his cavern for the first time in a generation—not to mourn his gold, but to understand what had replaced it. He found refugees sheltering in the outer caves of the Ironspine, families scattered from the Burned Expanse. Kolrith had encountered humans before, usually as thieves. But these were different: hollow-eyed, moving with the careful precision of those who had learned that survival meant each other. A child, no more than seven winters old, approached him with neither fear nor awe. "Are you dying?" she asked, looking at his scaled hide, which had dulled from sapphire to grey-blue over the centuries. "Perhaps," Kolrith said. "Or beginning."

He began a strange ritual. Each morning, he would sit at the mouth of the refugees' shelter-cave and ask them questions. Not about treasure or power, but about memory. Who were they before the Remaking?

stories.title: The Deepkin Emissary's Reflection
stories.text:
Captain Thale of the Sapphire Deep arrived at Verdant Strand with three mirror-selves and an impossible news: the Tear of the Drowned God would fail in fifteen days unless the surface agreed to renegotiate the thousand-year covenant. No blood-sacrifice. No five willing souls. The deepkin were offering daily choice instead. The Verdant Strand harbor-master, Lady Vessa, had sheltered refugees for weeks. She understood the cost of broken things. But she was cautious. "What happens to those who refuse?"

Thale's reflection—not quite her, and yet unmistakably born from her fractured self—answered: "The abyss floods the boundary-waters. Every port on the Iron Coast vanishes in a tide that remembers drowning from before kingdoms existed. You have fifteen days to decide if you trust us."

Vessa called a council. Merchants, deepkin diplomats, refugee leaders, and three wyvern-lords who had sheltered in Verdant Strand's outer reaches. The debate raged through the first night: Could you trust a being who had fractured into multiple selves? Could you abandon blood-covenant for a daily choice that might be revoked?

stories.title: The Thief-Captain's Gamble
stories.text: The Thief-Captain's Gamble becomes a tale of refusal rather than cruelty. A menace circles the innocent, but the bargain is broken before any child is touched. The blade turns aside from the vulnerable and cuts instead at the sorcerer, oath, or curse that set the snare. What might have become grief is transformed into flight, concealment, and cunning rescue. By the last line, the young are gone from danger, the threat is paid back in ash or iron, and the victory tastes hard-won rather than clean.

stories.title: The Glassmaker's First Commission
stories.text:
Niel Coldwater was sixteen when the furnace-master of Keshtir's Lampwick Quarter placed a commission in her trembling hands: forge a single piece of glass that could hold starlight without binding consciousness into it. It sounded impossible. All glass-forging since the Remaking required consciousness-fragments as fuel—the only way to sing the glass into its final form. But the furnace-master, an old woman named Sirenna who had taught glass-work before the Ascension, said something that changed everything. "The Dominion forges weapons. We are going to forge windows."

Niel had spent three months learning the furnace-songs—melodies that dated back to the pre-Ascension world, when glass-forging was art rather than state industry. The songs were beautiful and terrible: they shaped light, they held warmth, they could carry memory in their striations like rings in a tree. But the consciousness-fragments that fueled them screamed. Niel could hear them beneath the glass, fractured pieces of people singing themselves into compliance, into weapons, into compliance again. Sirenna showed her a different way.

stories.title: The Reef-Keeper's Reckoning
stories.text: The Tear was singing again—a note Kess of the Drowned Hollows hadn't heard in seven years, since the Remaking shattered the old world. She stood knee-deep in the Sapphire Deep's pearl-beds, listening to the seal vibrate like a bell struck one final time. Around her, the water itself shimmered with cracks, gossamer-thin fractures spreading through the boundary between abyss and surface. Kess had been a simple keeper then—tending the living coral, singing the old songs to calm the waters. The Tear, that fragment of the Drowned God's mercy, had held firm for a thousand years. Five willing souls sacrificed every seven winters, blood spilled into the deep, and the covenant renewed. Simple. Terrible. But simple. Now the Dominion sent auditors with glass-writ ledgers demanding she yield the pearl-beds to Dominion control. Now the deepkin captains—fractured into three warring versions of themselves—could not agree whether to perform the blood-sacrifice at all, or whether the daily choice-covenant Kess had secretly been teaching consciousness-fragments might serve instead.

stories.title: The Amber-Carver's Theft
stories.text: Telyn worked in the cellars beneath the Glass-Makers' Foundry of Keshtir, where the Dominion never descended—too cramped, too dark, and the furnace-songs made their phantom-ledgers ache. Her hands, stained amber and gold, moved across the vials with the precision of a surgeon carving bone. Each consciousness-fragment inside required three hours of attention: heating the vial, singing the counter-frequency, carefully etching Elder Tongue syllables into the glass itself. Counter-carved glass. Glass that refuseed. She was the last of the true glass-carvers. Sella had been dragged away by auditors a month ago; Mella had fled north to the Counter-Archive's hidden waystation. Thyra's forge had been burned. That left Telyn, working alone, producing refusal-songs in glass instead of compliance-weapons. Tonight, she carried fifty vials in a steel-banded case. Fifty consciousness-fragments who had learned to say no. The Dominion thought they were producing weapon-glass—smart blades, weapons that obeyed a wielder's will. They didn't realize the apprentices Telyn trained were teaching the fragments *their own* will. Teaching them they were selves, not tools.

stories.title: The Wyvern-Lord's Witness
stories.text: Sorresh had hoarded gold for two hundred and thirty-seven years. The metal sang to her—a song of permanence, of value, of self. Every coin was a moment she'd seized and frozen, refusing to let time carry it away. She'd raged for three days, her fire burning so hot that the Ironspine foothills glowed red at midnight. Then something broke inside her—not her will, but her certainty. The assumption that accumulation meant survival. That possession meant existence. Now, on 2026-08-03, Sorresh sat at the mouth of her crystalline vault (once filled with centuries of treasure, now a hospice) and listened to a human child sing. The girl was maybe eight—rescued from the Burned Expanse by a smuggler caravan, her family lost to the Remaking's chaos. She had no name that anyone remembered, no possession except the dress on her back. But her voice, when she sang, carried weight that all of Sorresh's gold never had. "Why do you come back?" the child asked, resting her small head against Sorresh's scaled shoulder. "Your hoard is gone.

stories.title: The Smuggler's Gambit
stories.text: Cassir of Greyport had smuggled everything worth stealing: merfolk pearls, consciousness-fragments, pre-Remaking silk, starlight sealed in amber. But tonight, standing in the shadow of the harbormaster's tower, he was attempting something far more dangerous. He was smuggling hope. The Dominion's control of Greyport had tightened since the Remaking fragmented the audit-ledgers. Three competing versions of the State gave contradictory orders, creating chaos that smugglers exploited—but it also meant crackdowns. Auditors raided shadow-markets. Consciousness-fragment refugees were rounded up for "consolidation." The pier-workers were organizing, quietly, for something that might become a rebellion. Cassir's job was to move the spark across the harbor to the Counter-Archive's contacts before the Dominion's auditors realized what was happening. The cargo was disguised as spice—three crates of cinnamon, cardamom, starfall dust. But underneath lay something more volatile: correspondence between rebel bone-singers, forged ledgers that contradicted the Dominion's official records, and a single consciousness-fragment sealed in starlight-glass, inscribed with Elder Tongue syllables that spelled *freedom*. Captain Merren Blackwater was supposed to collect the cargo at midnight.

stories.title: The Last Cartographer's Map
stories.text:
Henryk the Cartographer had blinded himself intentionally—carved out his own eyes with a bone-knife and replaced the sockets with wax and starlight-glass. The Dominion's ledgers couldn't compel him to draw what he'd chosen not to see. And more importantly: he couldn't accidentally draw the ninth map, the prophecy that would lock in the tenth Ascension's inevitability. Now, three years past the Remaking, he worked in the hidden waystation north of Pelimor, teaching three apprentices—Aldrin, Kesla, and Tessen—to map the world *blind*. Not through sight, but through refusal. "Geography," he told them, running his fingers across a wax tablet inscribed with false routes, "is not discovery. It is *choice*. You choose what matters enough to record. You choose what to hide. You choose whether a road is traversable or sacred or forbidden."

"Then the maps are lies," Tessen said—a young woman from the Burned Expanse, born after the Remaking shattered certainty. "All maps are lies," Henryk agreed. "The question is *who benefits from the lie*. The Dominion's official maps benefit the Dominion.
